name: Ireland
tagline: English-speaking, EU, and your IB score becomes a number
summary: Ireland is English-speaking and inside the EU, and it converts your overall IB score into CAO points on a published table, and courses are filled strictly by points. As an EU citizen who has lived in the EEA you normally pay no tuition at all under the Free Fees Initiative - only the student contribution, which fell to 2,500 EUR from 2026/27. The catch is that you apply through one central office, CAO, with a closing date of 1 February, and that Irish student accommodation is expensive and scarce.
whyConsider: Everything is taught in English, so there is no language barrier and no language test to plan for.
The IB-to-CAO conversion is published and public: you can work out before you apply roughly which courses your predicted score reaches.

Free Fees Initiative: EU/EEA/Swiss/UK nationals ordinarily resident in the EEA for three of the previous five years pay no tuition on a first undergraduate degree, only the 2,500 EUR student contribution.
A grade 4 or better in Higher Level Mathematics adds 25 bonus CAO points, which is worth roughly a whole IB point.
One application, one fee, up to ten Level 8 course choices in preference order.
watchOuts: CAO closes at 17:00 on 1 February - months before you sit your exams, and you are applying on predicted performance with no idea of the year's points.
Points requirements are not published in advance. They are set each August by supply and demand, so a course that needed 510 points last year can need 543 this year.
Accommodation in Dublin is expensive and in short supply; purpose-built student housing can run well over 1,000 EUR a month and campus rooms are allocated by lottery in many universities.
The 2,500 EUR student contribution is the maximum rate for 2026/27, after a permanent 500 EUR cut in Budget 2026. It is set politically each year, so confirm the 2027/28 amount before you commit.
The CAO IB conversion table is republished every year for that year's entry. The table below is the one for 2026 entry; check the 2027 version when it appears (usually in late 2026).

ibRecognition.minimumPoints: 24 points and the award of the full IB Diploma. For a Level 8 honours bachelor's degree the minimum is 24 overall including 3 subjects at grade 5 at Higher Level and 3 subjects at grade 4 at Standard Level (the '3 H5' matriculation route), or 24 overall with the Diploma awarded where only '2 H5' is required. Level 7/6 courses require 24 overall and the award of the Diploma.
ibRecognition.subjectLevelRule: The CAO's agreed table compares IB subject grades to Irish Leaving Certificate grades for meeting subject requirements. Higher Level: IB 7 = H1, 6 = H2, 6 = H3, 5 = H4, 5 = H5, 4 = H6, 3 = H7. Standard Level: IB 7 = O1, 6 = O2, 6 = O3, 5 = O4, 5 = O5, 4 = O6. Where a course asks for O6, a grade 4 at Standard Level is the pass mark. This table is used ONLY for meeting subject requirements, never for calculating points.
ibRecognition.gradeConversion: Points are awarded on your overall IB score from a single sitting. IB 45 = 600; 44 = 600; 43 = 594; 42 = 577; 41 = 565; 40 = 553; 39 = 541; 38 = 520; 37 = 508; 36 = 497; 35 = 481; 34 = 466; 33 = 453; 32 = 442; 31 = 430; 30 = 412; 29 = 400; 28 = 389; 27 = 379; 26 = 368; 25 = 359; 24 = 350. The CAO notes these are sample grades and the steps between them are not even, because they are based on statistical comparison with the Leaving Certificate.
notes: Bonus points: 25 additional CAO points for a grade 4 or better in Higher Level Mathematics, provided mathematics is included in the overall award used for the points calculation.
Single sitting only. All subjects must be examined at the same time and points are calculated from that one sitting.

Minimum English: IB English A grade 3 at HL or 4 at SL; English B grade 4 at HL or 6 at SL (4 at either level if you present the IB through English); Literature and Performance 3 at HL or 4 at SL with documentation that it was the English option.

Mathematics: both Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation are acceptable, but the CAO document strongly recommends Analysis and Approaches where a course has a Higher Level maths requirement, and says some institutions may make it mandatory.
Ask your IB coordinator to list 'Central Applications Office' among the institutions permitted to access your results, so CAO can pull your May 2027 results directly on release day.
The IB Career-related Certificate is accepted only for Level 6/7 courses in related areas and is scored to a maximum of 390 points.

deadlines.label: CAO application facility opens for 2027 entry
deadlines.notes: Published twice: the last line of the CAO Timetable of Events reads "5th November 2026 - CAO application facility opens for 2027 applications", and the CAO Handbook 2027 gives "CAO online application facility opens on 5 November at 12:00 noon". Nothing can be submitted before midday.

deadlines.label: Discounted application fee ends - 35 EUR becomes 50 EUR
deadlines.notes: The discounted online fee ends at 17:00 (CAO Handbook 2027, Timetable of Events and Table 1.1). Missing it costs 15 EUR, not your place: you can still apply at the normal 50 EUR until 1 February. The fee ladder is in Table 1.1 of the CAO Handbook 2027 and is the part most often got wrong: early online (discounted) 35 EUR by 20 January, normal online 50 EUR by 1 February, late online 65 EUR by 1 May, Change of Mind nil. Amending your course choices between 5 February and 1 March costs a further 10 EUR. Application fees are non-refundable and CAO states that no extension to any closing date is allowed.

deadlines.label: HPAT registration closes - CAO and the test board publish different dates for this
deadlines.notes: No date is recorded here, deliberately, because the two official publishers disagree and the cheaper reading costs a medicine place. CAO’s Timetable of Events lists, against "HPAT Test - Undergraduate Entry to Medicine", a "Registration Window: 5th November - 1st February". ACER, which actually runs the test and takes the registration, says on its own registration page: "Your online registration and payment must be completed by: 5:15pm GMT 16 January 2026", with "Late registrations will be accepted up to 5.15pm GMT 26 January 2026" for an additional fee, and an exceptional late registration available only to applicants who have already applied to CAO. Both pages were read on 23 September 2026 and both are live. A student who trusts CAO’s page has already missed ACER’s standard closing date by a fortnight and its late date by a week. Neither publisher had put up 2027 dates by 23 September 2026, which is why the state here is "not yet announced" rather than a date. What to do instead: register with ACER, not CAO, and treat mid-January 2027 as the real deadline; the 2026 standard registration fee was 164 EUR. Your HPAT result reaches CAO automatically - the CAO Handbook says "Current year HPAT results will be obtained directly from ACER" - so the registration is the only thing you have to do yourself.

deadlines.label: Normal closing date - the one that matters
deadlines.notes: CAO publishes this as "1st February (17:00) - Normal closing date for applications". Confirmed for 2027 entry by the CAO Handbook 2027 (Timetable of Events and Table 1.1), read on 24 September 2026; the Timetable of Events web page still shows the 2026 cycle. The fee at this point is 50 EUR. Restricted-entry courses - those with a test, interview, portfolio or audition, including undergraduate medicine - must be on your course choices list by now, with one narrow escape: the handbook allows them to be "added to your application using the facility to amend course choices (for a fee of 10) before 1 March at 5pm". They cannot be introduced during the free Change of Mind window in May and June, except where a restricted course shares the exact same assessment procedures as one you already listed. The CAO Handbook also advises applying online before this date and time if you need to sit HPAT or GAMSAT.

deadlines.label: Facility to amend course choices opens - 10 EUR
deadlines.notes: Course choices can be amended online from 12:00 on this day for a €10 fee; source: CAO Handbook 2027, Timetable of Events and Table 1.1. Nothing can be changed between 1 February and this day.

deadlines.label: HPAT test window - CAO and the test board publish different windows for this
deadlines.notes: The same disagreement as the registration date, on the same two pages. CAO’s Timetable of Events gives "Test sitting: 13th February - 16th February". ACER says "The HPAT - Ireland test window will run across a number of days from 13-22 February 2026". A student who blocks out only CAO’s four days may be sitting the test on a day they have given away. Both pages were read on 23 September 2026; neither had published a 2027 window, so no date is recorded. What to do instead: take the sitting date from the confirmation ACER sends you at registration, and keep the second half of February 2027 clear until you have it.

deadlines.label: Closing date for amending course choices - last chance to add a restricted course
deadlines.notes: CAO publishes this as "1st March (17:00) - Closing date for amending course choices". Confirmed for 2027 entry by the CAO Handbook 2027 (Timetable of Events and Table 1.1), read on 24 September 2026; the Timetable of Events web page still shows the 2026 cycle. After this time no restricted-entry course can be added to your application for the rest of the cycle: the free Change of Mind window that opens in May cannot introduce them, and a late application cannot include them either. If undergraduate medicine, or an art, design, architecture, music or drama course with a portfolio or audition, is not on your list by now, it is not available to you this year.

deadlines.label: Late application window - 65 EUR, and no restricted courses
deadlines.notes: CAO publishes this as two lines, "5th March (12:00) - Late application facility opens" and "1st May (17:00) - Closing date for late applications"; the time shown here is the closing one, because that is the one that costs something. Confirmed for 2027 entry by the CAO Handbook 2027 (Timetable of Events and Table 1.1), read on 24 September 2026; the Timetable of Events web page still shows the 2026 cycle. The fee is 65 EUR. Restricted-entry courses cannot be applied for at all in this window, and the handbook warns that individual institutions may refuse late applications outright: "mature applicants, and those presenting qualifications other than recently taken EU school-leaving examinations, should check the relevant HEI website before making a late application". An IB Diploma completed the same summer is a recently taken EU school-leaving examination, but the institution decides, not CAO.

deadlines.label: Change of Mind opens - free, and unlimited
deadlines.notes: CAO publishes this as "5th May (12:00) - Online Change of Mind facility becomes available (Free)". The CAO Handbook 2027, read on 24 September 2026, gives this day and time but marks it "(expected date)", so it stays provisional. You may use it as many times as you like to introduce, remove or reorder courses, but each Change of Mind "cancels and supersedes all previous course choices in any category in which changes are made", so the list you leave behind is the list that is read. Restricted-entry courses cannot be introduced here.

deadlines.label: Change of Mind closes - your final order of preference
deadlines.notes: CAO publishes this as "1st July (17:00) - Change of Mind closes". Confirmed for 2027 entry by the CAO Handbook 2027 (Timetable of Events and Table 1.1), read on 24 September 2026; the Timetable of Events web page still shows the 2026 cycle. This is the date the whole Irish system turns on, because offers follow your stated order of preference exactly and this is the last moment you can change it. It closes a few days before IB results are released in early July, so the order you submit is an order you choose without knowing your score. Decide it against your predicted grades and against last year’s points for each course, not against a result you do not have yet.

deadlines.label: IB free results requests close - make sure CAO is on your coordinator’s list
deadlines.notes: The IB’s cut-off: before 5 July your coordinator sends your results to up to six institutions free of charge; after 5 July you request them yourself through rrs.ibo.org at $19 each, with processing quoted at up to 14 working days and longer in the July–September peak. The IB does not say what happens on 5 July itself, so have it done by 4 July 2027. CAO needs it: the CAO Handbook 2027 says "If you are an IB candidate for May 2027: Ask your school's IB Coordinator to add "Central Applications Office (CAO)" to the list of institutions allowed to access your results", and asks for your IB candidate number so the results can be matched. If it is not done, CAO never receives your results and you are not considered, whatever your score. CAO counts as one of the six, exactly as UCAS does in the IB’s own example, and a late request can turn into a missed 1 August Round One cut-off rather than just a fee. Ask the coordinator before study leave begins, in writing, and ask them to confirm CAO is on the list.

deadlines.label: Your IB results must reach CAO to be read in Round One
deadlines.notes: The CAO entry-requirements booklet for EU/EFTA/UK applicants says: "Results should arrive with CAO no later than 1 August. We cannot guarantee that results received after that will be processed in time for inclusion in Round 1. Inclusion in later rounds is subject to availability of places." The general rule behind it is "documents should be with CAO 12 days before the relevant offer round". Published as "1 August" with no year, in a booklet dated November 2025 for 2026 entry; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. If your coordinator has listed CAO as an institution permitted to see your results this happens by itself when results are released in early July; if not, you must upload or post them, with an English translation where the document is not in English, and with your CAO number on every page. Missing it does not end the application - it moves you out of Round One and into whatever places are left. The CAO Handbook 2027 states the general rule for this cycle: results "must arrive in CAO a minimum of 12 days before the relevant offer round".

deadlines.label: Round One offers - the round an IB candidate is in
deadlines.notes: Not yet announced: the CAO Handbook 2027 lists Round One as "(TBC)" and its timetable says "Round One offers (date to be confirmed)"; the round dates move each year with the Irish Leaving Certificate results they wait for. For 2026 entry the published dates were Round A on 6 July at 10:00, Round 0 on 6 August at 10:00, Leaving Certificate results on 21 August, and Round One on 26 August at 14:00, with Rounds 2 to 5 through September. Round One is the one that matters to you: the CAO Handbook says "Applicants applying on the basis of school leaving examination results/grades, regardless of the year completed, will compete for an offer in Round One". Round A is for deferred, mature and Access applicants and those needing visa time, and Round Zero for graduate-entry medicine and QQI quota applicants - an IB candidate applying straight from school is in neither, so an empty inbox in July and early August means nothing has gone wrong. The booklet is blunt about why: "EU applicants are considered in competition with Irish school leavers. Consequently, offers cannot issue until the 2026 Irish school leaving results are known."

deadlines.label: Round One acceptance closes - about six days after the offer
deadlines.notes: The least visible date in the Irish system and the one that actually loses places. An offer is not a place until you accept it online: "If you receive an offer and you choose to accept this offer, you must do so online by the reply date indicated on the Offer email." For 2026 entry the gap was six days - Round One offers at 14:00 on 26 August, "Round 1 acceptances closing date" at 15:00 on 1 September - and the other rounds were tighter still, two or three days each. The 2027 dates were not published as of 23 September 2026, so no date is recorded; expect late August or early September and expect under a week. Two things worth knowing before the email arrives: you may accept only one offer per round, from either the Level 8 or the Level 7/6 list, and accepting a lower preference does not remove you from consideration for the higher preferences you listed above it in later rounds.

deadlines.label: Later offer rounds and the end of the offer season
deadlines.notes: Not getting an offer in Round One is not the end of the cycle. For 2026 entry CAO ran Rounds 2 to 5 on 7, 15, 22 and 29 September, each with its own acceptance date two days later, and the "Offer Season Ends" line fell on 1 October. An Available Places facility, for courses still unfilled, opened the day after Round One and is free to existing applicants. The 2027 dates were not published as of 23 September 2026.

steps: From 5 November 2026, register on cao.ie and start your application; pay by 20 January 2027 to get the 35 EUR discounted fee rather than 50 EUR.
List up to ten Level 8 (honours bachelor’s) courses and up to ten Level 7/6 courses, strictly in the order you actually want them - Irish offers follow your preference order exactly.

Include any restricted-entry course (medicine, some art and design, some performance courses) before the 1 February closing date, or add it for 10 EUR through the amend-course-choices facility before 1 March; after that it cannot be added at all.
If you are applying for undergraduate medicine, register for HPAT with ACER, not with CAO, and work to ACER’s mid-January closing date rather than the later one on CAO’s timetable.

Ask your IB coordinator to list the Central Applications Office among the institutions permitted to see your results, and give CAO your IB candidate number, so your results reach CAO automatically in July 2027.
Use the free Change of Mind window from 5 May to 1 July 2027 to settle your final order of preference - it closes before your IB results arrive.
Results are released in early July; CAO converts your overall IB score to points on its own published scale and matches you against the cut-off for each course in your order of preference.
If your results do not reach CAO by 1 August they may miss Round One, so check your CAO account rather than assuming.
Accept your Round One offer online by the reply date on the offer email - roughly six days - and apply for accommodation immediately.
application.selectionNotes: Almost everything is decided by points. CAO ranks all applicants for each course and the cut-off is simply the points of the last person offered a place, which is why the requirement is only known after the fact. An IB Diploma is converted on CAO’s own published scale, which is not linear: 45 points is 600, 40 is 553, 36 is 497, 30 is 412 and 24 - the minimum for the award of the diploma and the floor for a Level 8 course - is 350. A further 25 points are added for a grade 4 or better in Higher Level Mathematics. The score must come from a single sitting. Exceptions to points-only selection: undergraduate medicine combines points with the HPAT test; some art, design, architecture, music and drama courses require a portfolio, audition or interview; and a small number of courses run interviews. Those are the "restricted" courses you must list by 1 February, or add by 1 March for 10 EUR.

language.englishTaughtBachelors: All of them. Ireland teaches its degree programmes in English; Irish (Gaeilge) is required only for a handful of courses such as primary teaching and Irish-language programmes.
language.englishProof: For IB students the CAO document sets the minimum directly: English A grade 3 at HL or 4 at SL; English B grade 4 at HL or 6 at SL (4 at either level if you are presenting the IB through English); Literature and Performance 3 at HL or 4 at SL with supporting documentation. Individual institutions and courses may set a higher bar, and applicants whose school-leaving examinations are more than two years old must supply additional proof of English.
notes: Primary school teaching requires Irish, which effectively closes that route to an IB student from Denmark.
Because your IB was taught in English, you should not normally need IELTS or TOEFL - but confirm with the individual institution, not with CAO.

tuitionEuEea.value: 0 EUR tuition under the Free Fees Initiative for eligible EU/EEA/Swiss/UK students on a first undergraduate degree, plus a student contribution charge of 2,500 EUR per year. Institutions also charge a small compulsory student levy, typically between 80 and 250 EUR.
tuitionEuEea.year: 2026/27 (2,500 EUR is the maximum student contribution after the permanent 500 EUR cut in Budget 2026; the 2027/28 figure had not been announced on 2026-09-24)

tuitionNonEu.value: Set by each institution. Trinity College Dublin, 2026/27, year 1: 22,580 EUR for arts, humanities and business courses and 29,570 EUR for science courses, with some health-science courses higher.

costs.applicationFee: 35 EUR online by 20 January 2027 (17:00), 50 EUR by the normal closing date of 1 February 2027 (17:00), 65 EUR for a late application by 1 May 2027 (17:00). Change of Mind is free; amending course choices between 5 February and 1 March costs 10 EUR. Fees are non-refundable (CAO Handbook 2027, Table 1.1).

livingCostMonthly.value: Trinity College Dublin estimates 19,937-29,050 EUR for an undergraduate academic year in Dublin, including accommodation (an annual figure; the page gives no monthly one). Galway, Cork and Limerick are cheaper.
livingCostMonthly.year: Estimate on the TCD page, last updated July 2026

notes: Non-EU tuition varies by university and subject; Trinity College Dublin is recorded above as an example. Check the fees page of each institution.
Living costs are published per university, not nationally. Trinity College Dublin is recorded above; expect Dublin to be considerably more expensive than Galway, Cork or Limerick.
Eligibility for free fees is assessed by the higher education institution you attend, not by CAO.

funding: Free Fees Initiative: the state pays your tuition if you are an EU/EEA/Swiss/UK national who has been ordinarily resident in an EU/EEA/Swiss state or the UK for at least three of the five years before entry, on a first full-time undergraduate course of at least two years. An EU/EEA citizen who has lived in Denmark for three of the five years before entry meets the residency test; years in another EU/EEA state, Switzerland or the UK count too.

funding.note: The programme must be SU-approved, and outside the Nordics SU is capped at four years (48 klip). Apply to Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen before you leave.

funding: SUSI grants cover the student contribution for students who meet Irish means and residency tests. Most students moving from Denmark will not meet the residency condition in their first year, so do not plan around it.
University entrance scholarships exist at most Irish universities but are small in number and usually awarded on results after entry.
As an EU citizen you can work in Ireland without a permit, and student jobs are widely available in Dublin, Cork and Galway.
workRights: As an EU/EEA citizen you have the right to work in Ireland with no permit and no hour limit. Non-EU students on Stamp 2 may work up to 20 hours a week in term time and 40 hours a week in June to September and from 15 December to 15 January, and must register their immigration permission each year and hold private health insurance.
residency: Nothing to arrange in advance as an EU citizen: you can enter with your EU/EEA passport or national ID card and stay to study with no visa or residence permit. Once you arrive, get a PPS number (Personal Public Service number) from the Department of Social Protection - you need it for a job, a bank account and most public services - and open an Irish bank account. Non-EU students need a visa or preclearance before travelling and must register with immigration and pay the residence permit fee.
housing: Treat this as the main financial risk of studying in Ireland. Dublin in particular has a long-running shortage of rental housing, and purpose-built student accommodation is priced well above a normal shared room. Apply for university-owned accommodation the same day you accept your offer - most Irish universities allocate first-year rooms quickly and several run a lottery when demand exceeds supply. If you miss campus housing, the realistic options are a shared house through Daft.ie, a room in a private student residence, or 'digs' (a room in a family home, often Monday to Friday only), which is common in Dublin and much cheaper. Cork, Galway, Limerick and Maynooth are all easier and cheaper than Dublin. No official national rent figure is quoted here.
healthcare: Bring your European Health Insurance Card from the country where you are insured; it covers medically necessary public treatment during your stay. EU students are not required to buy private health insurance. Note that Ireland charges for GP visits unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card, so budget for that, and most universities run a low-cost student health service on campus. Non-EU students must hold private health insurance as a condition of their immigration permission.

institutions.name: Trinity College Dublin
institutions.note: Ireland's oldest and most internationally recognised university, on a walled city-centre campus; its high-points courses are among the hardest in the country to reach.

institutions.name: University College Dublin
institutions.note: The largest university in Ireland, on a suburban campus at Belfield, with broad first-year entry routes that let you specialise later.

institutions.name: University of Galway
institutions.note: A river-side campus in a small, very sociable west-coast city, with noticeably cheaper living costs than Dublin.

institutions.name: University College Cork
institutions.note: A green campus in Ireland's second city, strong in food, pharma and life sciences with a big multinational employer base nearby.

institutions.name: University of Limerick
institutions.note: A true campus university with a large amount of on-campus student housing and a co-operative education programme that builds paid placements into most degrees.

institutions.name: Dublin City University
institutions.note: Modern, industry-facing and built around paid work placements; cheaper to live near than the city-centre universities.

institutions.name: Maynooth University
institutions.note: A small campus town half an hour from Dublin, with flexible arts and science degrees that let you keep several subjects going into second year.

institutions.name: RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences
institutions.note: A specialist health-sciences institution with a very international student body; EU applicants to medicine apply through CAO and sit the HPAT.

institutions.name: Technological University Dublin
institutions.note: Ireland's largest technological university, practice-focused, with many Level 7 routes that ladder into Level 8 degrees if your points fall short.

institutions.name: Munster Technological University
institutions.note: A hands-on alternative to the research universities in the south, with lower points requirements and strong local industry links.

institutions.name: Atlantic Technological University
institutions.note: Spread across the north-west and west coast, with lower living costs than Dublin and easier entry points.

institutions.name: South East Technological University
institutions.note: A regional technological university in the south-east; a realistic option if your predicted points do not reach the Dublin universities.

institutions.name: National College of Art and Design
institutions.note: Ireland's national art school; entry is a restricted-entry CAO course combining points with a portfolio submission, so it must be listed by 1 February.

institutions.name: Dundalk Institute of Technology
institutions.note: A small institute between Dublin and Belfast with low points requirements and unusually strong music technology provision.
